source.title: Where Do Legal Factors Live in LLMs?

record.tranche_reason: Extends sparse-feature readout analysis to expert-defined legal factors in three pretrained LLMs; it does not reproduce the original toy-model superposition experiment.
record.gate_note: The study tests whether full activations and selected SAE features predict legal-factor labels. It does not test superposition geometry, feature sparsity or importance as causal determinants, or whether features compete for capacity. The TF-IDF comparison concerns wording, and the full-vector probe results alone do not establish that features are distributed across neurons. The Figure 3 per-factor location inventory is not transcribed in full; aggregate readout results and the explicitly discussed F14 tradeoff are recorded.
record.test_reason: The study uses released SAEs (Qwen-Scope, Gemma Scope) as a tool and reports how well its own selected-feature readouts predict legal-factor labels. It does not compare SAE features with a neuron basis. It does not measure how features are spread across neurons, superposition geometry or capacity. Its stability test checks its own feature-selection procedure under resampling of training passages, not whether SAE features are canonical across decompositions. TF-IDF is near-perfect on the same task, so high readout AUC shows that wording-level information is present, not that the model stores sparse superposed features. None of its results bear on whether any version holds.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that all 26 CATO factors are linearly readable from full activations in three models, and that one or a few selected SAE features retain much of this information. They report 78 layer–feature coordinates and note that related factors sometimes share a feature. They frame the work as a proof of concept on controlled narratives, and note that TF-IDF also performs near-perfectly.
record.recipe_differences: This is an SAE-feature and linear-probe readout study on legal-factor labels, not a reproduction of the original toy-model superposition method. It uses fixed pretrained model weights and fits separate classifiers to controlled passages.
record.method_sensitivity: Model and readout size affect aggregate AUC. Selected factor locations vary by layer. In Qwen3-8B, selected feature sets vary under resampling for F2, F8, F11, and F24.

fits_no_version.finding: Label-selected single SAE features (best layer) predict expert-defined legal factors with test AUC 0.86–1.00 across three models; random 5-feature sets are near chance; TF-IDF is also near-perfect.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Individual SAE features from public dictionaries align with human-defined domain concepts well enough to serve as compact linear readouts.

fits_no_version.finding: The same SAE feature is the best single readout for two related legal factors in several models (e.g., F16/F25 share L7/f20148 in Qwen3-1.7B; F24/F27 share a feature in Qwen3-8B and Gemma-2 2B). Feature selection varies under resampling for 4/26 factors, while readout weights stay similar.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Selected SAE features can respond to several related concepts, and label-based selection of SAE features is only partly stable.

record.problems: Evidence is from controlled English narratives about U.S. trade-secret factors, not naturally occurring cases; the authors note that positive and negative passages can differ in length and that TF-IDF performs strongly. The models are described as small by current standards. The study tests predictive readouts rather than whether selected SAE features causally support model behavior or are complete, canonical representational units.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 3 reports selected layer-feature coordinates and test AUCs for all 26 factors in each of three models (78 entries). Those individual entries are not transcribed here; the record includes the aggregate comparisons and the explicitly discussed F14 single-versus-five-feature results.

untested.parts: All: no toy models, sparsity transition or geometry.
All: no capacity or importance analysis.
All: no analysis of neuron polysemanticity.
No neuron-basis comparison or distributedness measure. The study does not test whether SAEs recover the model's sparse features rather than serving as a readout tool.
Completeness, canonicity and stability across SAE decompositions are not tested; the resampling checks only the study's own feature selection.
All: dimensionality of features is not examined.

record.verdict_notes: Reclassified from tests/T3 to uses_without_test/T4. The SAEs are a fixed tool, and all rows report the study's own readout performance or its own selection stability. Layer selection uses the test set, so per-factor best-layer AUCs are optimistic; the middle-layer comparisons in Figure 2 are not affected. The study cites Toy Models of Superposition only as background for SAEs.

versions.untested_parts: Toy-model overlap geometry, a sparsity-dependent transition, and regular geometry.
Capacity competition, dedicated dimensions for important features, and sharing by less important features.
Whether polysemanticity arises for reasons other than capacity pressure.

The study tests whether selected SAE features can predict legal-factor labels, but does not test whether features are spread across many neurons or whether this result generalizes beyond controlled English legal narratives.
Resampling tests selection stability for Qwen3-8B; completeness and canonicality are not established, and stability across different SAE decompositions or broadly across models is not tested.
Whether represented features are one-dimensional directions in the sense required by superposition, rather than multidimensional features.
